Wickard v. Filburn. The 1942 Supreme Court decision upholding federal agricultural regulation under the Commerce Clause. Roscoe Filburn, an Ohio farmer, planted more wheat than allowed under New Deal agricultural quotas and claimed he grew the excess for personal use, not interstate commerce. The Court ruled that the aggregate effect of many farms growing excess wheat for personal consumption affects the national wheat market and interstate commerce.

Justice Robert Jackson wrote that even wholly intrastate, non-commercial activity can be regulated if it substantially affects interstate commerce. The decision effectively abandoned the direct and indirect effects test, replacing it with an aggregate effects standard vastly expanding federal power. This became the foundation for virtually all post-1942 federal economic regulation, including labor, civil rights, environmental, and consumer protection laws. It marked the end of the Lochner era's limits on federal commerce power. The Commerce Clause no longer meaningfully constrains Congress. The decision shifted the balance of state and federal power decisively toward the federal government, fundamentally reimagining the Constitution's powers to Congress.
